# Model Evaluation and Validation

##### 99.7% accurate, zero fraud caught

A student in Bhubaneswar built a credit-card fraud detector for a portfolio project. The dataset had 284,807 transactions, of which 492 were fraudulent — 0.17%.

Her model reported 99.7% accuracy. She put it on her CV.

An interviewer asked to see the confusion matrix. It looked like this:

```
                 Predicted
                 Not fraud  Fraud
Actual Not fraud   284,315      0
       Fraud           492      0
```

The model predicted "not fraud" for every single transaction. It caught nothing. And because 99.83% of transactions genuinely are not fraud, always saying "not fraud" scores 99.83% accuracy — her model was actually *worse* than that trivial baseline.

Accuracy on imbalanced data is not a weak metric. It is an actively misleading one. Building a model is the easy part; knowing whether it is any good is the actual skill, and it starts with choosing a metric that can tell you.

##### The confusion matrix

Every classification metric derives from four counts:

```
                      Predicted
                  Negative  Positive
Actual Negative     TN        FP      ← FP = false alarm (Type I error)
       Positive     FN        TP      ← FN = missed case (Type II error)
```

```python
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, ConfusionMatrixDisplay
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred)
tn, fp, fn, tp = cm.ravel()
print(f"TN {tn}  FP {fp}  FN {fn}  TP {tp}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 5))
ConfusionMatrixDisplay(cm, display_labels=["not fraud", "fraud"]).plot(ax=ax, cmap="Blues")
```

**Print the confusion matrix before any metric.** It is four numbers and it tells you immediately whether a class is being ignored entirely — which is exactly what a single accuracy figure hides.

Which error matters more is a business question, not a statistical one. In fraud detection, a missed fraud (FN) costs the transaction value while a false alarm (FP) costs a few minutes of review. In cancer screening, a missed case is catastrophic and a false positive means an unnecessary follow-up test. Those asymmetries should drive everything.

##### Classification metrics

```
Accuracy  = (TP + TN) / total          What fraction did I get right?
Precision = TP / (TP + FP)             Of what I flagged, how much was real?
Recall    = TP / (TP + FN)             Of what was real, how much did I catch?
F1        = 2 · (P · R) / (P + R)      Harmonic mean of the two
Specificity = TN / (TN + FP)           Of the negatives, how many did I clear?
```

```python
from sklearn.metrics import (accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score,
                             f1_score, classification_report)

print(f"accuracy  {accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred):.4f}")
print(f"precision {precision_score(y_test, y_pred, zero_division=0):.4f}")
print(f"recall    {recall_score(y_test, y_pred):.4f}")
print(f"f1        {f1_score(y_test, y_pred):.4f}")
print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred, digits=3, zero_division=0))
```

The intuition worth carrying: **precision is about trust, recall is about coverage.** High precision means when the model raises a flag, believe it. High recall means the model rarely misses a real case.

They trade off. Flag everything and recall hits 100% while precision collapses. Flag only the single most certain case and precision hits 100% while recall approaches zero. **F1** balances them via the harmonic mean, which — unlike the arithmetic mean — punishes imbalance: precision 1.0 and recall 0.0 gives F1 = 0, not 0.5.

```python
# In the Bhubaneswar case
print(precision_score(y_test, y_pred, zero_division=0))   # 0.0 — nothing flagged
print(recall_score(y_test, y_pred))                        # 0.0 — nothing caught
print(accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred))                      # 0.9983 — meaningless
```

Three numbers, and only one of them looks good. That is the argument in a single line.

Which to optimise:

| Situation | Prioritise | Because |
|---|---|---|
| Fraud, disease screening | **Recall** | Missing a case is expensive |
| Spam filtering, content removal | **Precision** | False positives anger users |
| Balanced costs | **F1** | Neither error dominates |
| Ranking for a limited review queue | **Precision@k** | You can only review k items |

For multi-class problems, `average="macro"` treats every class equally (so a collapsed rare class shows up), while `average="weighted"` weights by class size and can hide it. Always print the per-class report as well.

##### ROC-AUC and precision-recall curves

Metrics above depend on a threshold. ROC and PR curves evaluate across *all* thresholds.

**ROC** plots true positive rate against false positive rate. **AUC** is the area underneath, interpretable as: the probability that a randomly chosen positive is ranked above a randomly chosen negative. 0.5 is random, 1.0 is perfect.

```python
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, roc_curve, average_precision_score, precision_recall_curve

probs = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_test, probs)
prec, rec, thr = precision_recall_curve(y_test, probs)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))
axes[0].plot(fpr, tpr, lw=2, label=f"AUC = {roc_auc_score(y_test, probs):.3f}")
axes[0].plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", lw=1, label="random")
axes[0].set_xlabel("False positive rate"); axes[0].set_ylabel("True positive rate")
axes[0].set_title("ROC curve"); axes[0].legend()

axes[1].plot(rec, prec, lw=2, label=f"AP = {average_precision_score(y_test, probs):.3f}")
axes[1].axhline(y_test.mean(), color="k", ls="--", lw=1,
                label=f"baseline = {y_test.mean():.4f}")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Recall"); axes[1].set_ylabel("Precision")
axes[1].set_title("Precision-Recall curve"); axes[1].legend()
fig.tight_layout()
```

**On imbalanced data, prefer the PR curve.** ROC's false positive rate has TN in its denominator, and when TN is enormous even thousands of false positives barely move it — so ROC-AUC stays comfortably high while the model is unusable. Precision has no TN term, so those false positives crush it immediately.

For the fraud data, a model can show ROC-AUC of 0.94 and average precision of 0.18. Both are correct; only the second reflects the user experience. Note that the PR baseline is the positive rate itself (0.0017 here), so 0.18 is genuinely 100× better than random — context that ROC never gives you.

Once you have the curve, choose a threshold deliberately:

```python
import numpy as np
f1s = 2 * prec * rec / (prec + rec + 1e-9)
best_thr = thr[int(np.argmax(f1s[:-1]))]
print(f"threshold maximising F1: {best_thr:.4f}")

# Or by business cost
def total_cost(threshold, cost_fn=18000, cost_fp=40):
    pred = (probs >= threshold).astype(int)
    fn = ((y_test == 1) & (pred == 0)).sum()
    fp = ((y_test == 0) & (pred == 1)).sum()
    return fn * cost_fn + fp * cost_fp

costs = [(t, total_cost(t)) for t in np.linspace(0.01, 0.99, 99)]
print(min(costs, key=lambda x: x[1]))
```

Tune the threshold on validation data, then report the resulting performance on test.

##### Regression metrics

```python
from sklearn.metrics import (mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error,
                             r2_score, mean_absolute_percentage_error)
import numpy as np

mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_pred)
mse = mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred)
rmse = np.sqrt(mse)
r2 = r2_score(y_test, y_pred)
mape = mean_absolute_percentage_error(y_test, y_pred)

print(f"MAE  {mae:,.2f}   (average error, same units as y)")
print(f"RMSE {rmse:,.2f}  (penalises large errors more)")
print(f"R²   {r2:.4f}     (fraction of variance explained)")
print(f"MAPE {mape:.2%}   (average percentage error)")
```

| Metric | Units | Outlier sensitive | Use when |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MAE** | Same as y | No | You want a robust, interpretable average error |
| **RMSE** | Same as y | Yes | Large errors are disproportionately bad |
| **MSE** | y squared | Very | Optimisation only — units are meaningless |
| **R²** | Unitless | Moderate | Comparing across datasets |
| **MAPE** | Percentage | Yes | Communicating to non-technical audiences |

**RMSE ≥ MAE always**, and the gap tells you about error distribution — a large gap means a few big errors dominate. Reporting both is more informative than either alone.

MAPE is intuitive but breaks when actual values are near zero (division by a tiny number) and it penalises over-prediction and under-prediction asymmetrically. Use it for communication, not for model selection.

Always compare against a baseline: predicting the mean for every row gives R² = 0 by definition. A model with R² = 0.05 is barely better than that.

##### k-fold cross-validation

A single train/test split gives one estimate, and that estimate depends on which rows happened to land in the test set. On small datasets the variation between splits can be several percentage points.

Cross-validation splits the data into k folds, trains k times with a different fold held out each time, and averages.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Training data] --> B[Split into 5 folds]
    B --> C[Fold 1 test, folds 2-5 train -> score 1]
    B --> D[Fold 2 test, others train -> score 2]
    B --> E[Fold 3 test, others train -> score 3]
    B --> F[Fold 4 test, others train -> score 4]
    B --> G[Fold 5 test, others train -> score 5]
    C --> H[Mean +/- std across folds]
    D --> H
    E --> H
    F --> H
    G --> H
```

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, cross_validate, StratifiedKFold

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
scores = cross_val_score(pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc")
print(f"ROC-AUC {scores.mean():.3f} ± {scores.std():.3f}")
print("per fold:", scores.round(3))

# Multiple metrics at once, plus training scores for a bias/variance read
results = cross_validate(pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=cv,
                         scoring=["roc_auc", "average_precision", "recall", "f1"],
                         return_train_score=True)
for k in ["test_roc_auc", "train_roc_auc", "test_recall", "test_f1"]:
    print(f"{k:18s} {results[k].mean():.3f} ± {results[k].std():.3f}")
```

**The standard deviation matters as much as the mean.** Scores of 0.82 ± 0.01 and 0.82 ± 0.09 describe very different models — the second is unstable, and its performance on your next batch of data is genuinely uncertain.

Choosing the right splitter:

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, StratifiedKFold, GroupKFold, TimeSeriesSplit

StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)   # classification — preserves class balance
KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)             # regression
GroupKFold(5)                                        # grouped data — same customer stays together
TimeSeriesSplit(5)                                   # temporal — always train on the past
```

Using plain `KFold` on time-series data lets the model train on the future to predict the past. Using it on grouped data lets the same customer appear in both train and validation. Both produce optimistic scores that collapse in production.

And **put preprocessing inside the pipeline**, so the scaler is refitted on each fold's training portion:

```python
# WRONG — the scaler saw all the data before CV started
X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_train)
cross_val_score(model, X_scaled, y_train, cv=5)

# CORRECT
pipe = Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()), ("clf", model)])
cross_val_score(pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=5)
```

##### The bias-variance trade-off

Total prediction error decomposes into three parts:

```
Error = Bias² + Variance + Irreducible noise
```

- **Bias** — error from wrong assumptions. A straight line fitted to curved data. High bias means **underfitting**.
- **Variance** — sensitivity to the particular training set. A deep tree that restructures when you change ten rows. High variance means **overfitting**.
- **Irreducible noise** — randomness no model can capture.

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import learning_curve, validation_curve

# Learning curve: does more data help?
sizes, train_sc, val_sc = learning_curve(
    pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc",
    train_sizes=np.linspace(0.1, 1.0, 10), random_state=42)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5))
axes[0].plot(sizes, train_sc.mean(1), "o-", label="train")
axes[0].plot(sizes, val_sc.mean(1), "s-", label="validation")
axes[0].fill_between(sizes, val_sc.mean(1) - val_sc.std(1),
                     val_sc.mean(1) + val_sc.std(1), alpha=0.2)
axes[0].set_xlabel("training examples"); axes[0].set_title("Learning curve"); axes[0].legend()

# Validation curve: what complexity is right?
depths = [1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 12, 20]
tr, va = validation_curve(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42), X_train, y_train,
                          param_name="max_depth", param_range=depths, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc")
axes[1].plot(depths, tr.mean(1), "o-", label="train")
axes[1].plot(depths, va.mean(1), "s-", label="validation")
axes[1].set_xlabel("max_depth"); axes[1].set_title("Validation curve"); axes[1].legend()
fig.tight_layout()
```

Diagnosing from the learning curve:

| Pattern | Diagnosis | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Both curves low, converged | High bias (underfitting) | More features, more complex model |
| Large persistent gap | High variance (overfitting) | More data, simpler model, regularisation |
| Validation still rising at the right edge | Need more data | Collect more |
| Curves converged at a good level | Well fitted | Ship it |

That third row is genuinely actionable — if the validation curve has flattened, collecting more data will not help and you should change the model instead.

##### Common mistakes

- Reporting accuracy on imbalanced data.
- Never printing the confusion matrix.
- ROC-AUC as the only metric when positives are rare.
- A single train/test split on a small dataset, mistaking split luck for performance.
- Reporting the CV mean without the standard deviation.
- Scaling or encoding outside the pipeline, leaking across folds.
- `KFold` on time-series or grouped data.
- Tuning the threshold on the test set.
- MAPE on data containing values near zero.
- Optimising a metric nobody asked for instead of the business cost.

##### Hands-on

Evaluate a classifier with the full set: confusion matrix, accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC-AUC and average precision. Then run 5-fold stratified cross-validation and compare the averaged score against your single-split estimate — note both the difference in the mean and the spread across folds. Deliberately construct an imbalanced version of your dataset (downsample the positive class to 2%) and reproduce the Bhubaneswar result, showing accuracy above 98% alongside recall of zero.

For the mini-project, build a complete evaluation report for a model: all relevant metrics with a short explanation of why each was chosen, a confusion matrix visualisation, both ROC and PR curves with baselines marked, a cross-validation score distribution shown as a box plot across folds, learning and validation curves, and a written diagnosis stating whether the model suffers from bias or variance and what you would do about it. Add a threshold analysis with a cost matrix — even invented costs force the right kind of thinking. End with a one-paragraph recommendation a manager could act on.

For the assignment, take a model on an imbalanced dataset and explain with numbers why accuracy is misleading and which metric better reflects performance. Show the majority-class baseline accuracy alongside your model's, and the confusion matrix for both. The comparison to the trivial baseline is the part that makes the argument undeniable.

##### Key takeaways

- Print the confusion matrix first; a single accuracy figure can hide a model that predicts one class always.
- Precision is trust, recall is coverage, and which matters is a business decision about error costs.
- On imbalanced data, use the precision-recall curve — ROC-AUC stays flatteringly high because of the huge TN count.
- Cross-validation gives a mean *and* a standard deviation; the spread tells you how stable the model is.
- Learning and validation curves diagnose bias versus variance and tell you whether more data will actually help.
